venue: **Preprint** — the footer of p1 reads "Preprint." Formatted for NeurIPS and carries the full NeurIPS Paper Checklist (pp29–35), and the code link is anonymized (`anonymous.4open.science`, p14), so this is an under-review NeurIPS submission posted to arXiv. Tagged `preprint`.
title: Two Stages of Folding: Convergent Mechanisms in AI Protein Folding Trunks
system: **general protein** — no protein family is targeted. Datasets are CATH Class 1 ("mainly α") domains and PISCES-culled X-ray chains (p15–16). Named examples are only PDB 6rwc (β-sheet) and 1l0s (left-handed β-helix), used for bias-map visualisation (p26).
n_targets: **200 activation-patching targets** (100 α-helical + 100 hairpin, lengths 100–400 residues, p16), drawn against **≈130,000 donor motif regions** from the PDB (p3), with 10 donors sampled per motif giving **≈10,000 patching experiments** (p3). Other sets: 200 α-helical proteins for the charge direction (p5), filtered from 5,000 CATH Class 1 chains (p16); 11,652 PISCES chains for hairpin mining (p16); 400 train / 200 eval proteins for distance probes (p7); ~500 steering cases per model (p6); 500 sampled β-hairpins for same-charge steering (p6); 600 proteins for the structure-module scaling analysis (p7); ≤40-residue single-motif proteins for the dose–response (p22). **No claim of generality beyond the two motifs studied is made** — the authors bound it themselves on p14.
method_class: **other** — mechanistic interpretability: activation patching + linear probing + representation steering + cross-model representational alignment (whitened Procrustes) and cross-model activation substitution. Not any of the corpus's conformational method classes.
backbones: **ESMFold, OpenFold, Boltz-1** — three head to head, in every analysis. Tag `multi-backbone`. Architectural relationships recorded in full in the section above; all three are AlphaFold-lineage.
templates: **NOT REPORTED** — templates are never mentioned as an input anywhere in the paper. ESMFold is template-free by construction; for OpenFold and Boltz-1 the template setting is never stated (protocol described p3, datasets p15–16). Do not assume off.
msa_handling: **DUAL — none + full (unspecified).** ESMFold takes a single sequence with no MSA; OpenFold and Boltz-1 take an MSA: "Both take a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) as input rather than a single sequence" (p3). **How those MSAs were built — search tool, database, depth, date — is NOT REPORTED anywhere**, which is a real reproducibility gap for the two MSA models given that MSA depth is known to move trunk representations. Not subsampled, not clustered, not state-filtered. Recycling is disabled throughout: "To simplify causal analysis, we disable recycling; for the short proteins considered, recycling provides minimal improvements (App. H)." (p3)
states_generated: **NOT APPLICABLE — no conformational generator.** The paper produces one deterministic structure per intervention condition (recycling disabled, p3); it never samples an ensemble, never targets two conformational states of one protein, and never scores state assignment. The two "states" toggled are **secondary-structure motifs of a local window** (β-hairpin vs helix-loop-helix, 12–25 residues, p14), not conformational states of a protein. If a single value is needed for the index: single-state per condition.
structural_priors_used: Substantial and entirely legitimate — all at design time, none in a prediction pipeline. (1) **PDB deposited structures** define every motif region: DSSP is run on deposited structures to identify motifs and align intervention windows (p3, p15). (2) **CATH Class 1 ("mainly α") domain list** selects the helical dataset (p15–16). (3) **PISCES culling set** `cullpdb_pc25.0_res0.0-2.5_len40-10000_R0.3_Xray_d2025_02_19_chains11652` (25% identity, X-ray, ≤2.5 Å, R ≤ 0.3) selects hairpin-bearing chains (p16). (4) **Deposited Cα coordinates supply the probe labels** — true pairwise Cα distance for distance probes and the 8 Å Cα contact definition (p7, p23). (5) **Structural-biology literature fixes two constants**: the 5.5 Å cross-strand Cα target distance is taken from Brändén & Tooze 1999 (p8), and the salt-bridge rationale for charge complementarity from Ciani et al. 2003 (p5). (6) **Motif-detection thresholds** (App E, p15) encode textbook hairpin/HLH geometry. None of this is a defect; it is what makes the intervention interpretable.
oracle_leakage:
**Overall: NONE FOUND on pipeline routes 1–5; a genuine selection effect on route 6; design-level (route 7) use is present and explicit.** Route by route:
**(1) Structures used as input or template — NONE FOUND.** No structure is given to any model as input; templates are never mentioned. What crosses into the forward pass is a *donor activation tensor*, computed by running the donor's **sequence** through the model, not the donor's coordinates. Protocol described p3: "We run both proteins through the folding trunk, extracting the sequence representation s^(k) and pairwise representation z^(k) at each block k. During the target's forward pass, we replace representations in the target's motif region with the donor's."
**(2) State annotations from a curated database driving templates or alignments — NONE FOUND as a pipeline route; present as dataset curation only.** DSSP, CATH and PISCES are used to *select and label* the protein sets (p15–16), not to bias any prediction. No GPCRdb/KLIFS/Kincore-style state annotation is used, and no alignment or template is state-annotated.
**(3) Cluster labels derived from known states — NONE FOUND.** No clustering is performed anywhere; protocol p3, p15–16.
**(4) Hyperparameters, sweeps, seeds or stopping criteria tuned against known states — NONE FOUND for the evaluation-set sense, but with a caveat that must be recorded.** The two constants that could have been tuned are not: the 5.5 Å distance target is taken from a textbook ("We choose 5.5Å as our target, the typical Cα–Cα spacing for cross-strand contacts in antiparallel β-sheets [Brändén and Tooze, 1999]", p8) and the 8 Å contact threshold is standard. **However, how the steering strengths α = 3σ (charge, p6) and α = 20σ (distance, p8) and the ablation/steering window sizes (15, 15, 10) were chosen is NOT REPORTED.** The dose–response sweep (p22) is run on a *separate* small single-motif set, explicitly to isolate the effect, so the sweep range itself is not fitted on the reported evaluation set — but the absence of any stated selection protocol for α means a reader cannot verify that the reported α was not picked because it worked.
**(5) Success defined post hoc by RMSD or TM to a structure they had — NONE FOUND, and this is the paper's cleanest rigour property.** Success is presence of the donor motif in the model's own output under an explicitly specified algorithm — DSSP codes, strand ≥2 residues, loop 0–5, adjacency for hairpins; DSSP code H, helix ≥4 residues, loop 2–8, adjacency for helix-loop-helix (App E, p15). No reference structure of a "correct answer" is ever compared against.
**(6) Best/worst model labels assigned against a held reference — NONE FOUND against a reference, but a real outcome-conditioned selection is present.** The single-block localisation analysis is run only on cases that already succeeded under a different intervention: verbatim, p4, "we repeat the patching experiment but intervene at a single block, patching either sequence or pairwise representations alone (**restricted to the ≈4,000 donor–target pairs where full patching was successful**)." The detailed §4.1 flow analysis narrows further: "We present the analysis in detail for ESMFold using **400 successful cases of block-0 sequence patching**" (p4). This is selection on the outcome of a prior intervention, not on a deposited structure, so it is not oracle leakage in the corpus sense — but every reported single-block success rate is conditional on full-trunk patching having worked, and the unconditional rate is lower and never given.
**(7) Design-level oracle use — PRESENT and explicit.** The expected answer is declared before the result is read, throughout. The donor→target design fixes what should appear ("we observe whether the output structure contains the donor motif in the patched region", p3); the charge intervention is constructed to reproduce a known biophysical effect ("the construction mimics the cross-strand electrostatic complementarity found in natural hairpins", p6); and the control conditions state their expected signs in advance ("**expecting** strands to repel … **expecting** strands to attract", p22). This is hypothesis-driven experimental design and is the *weaker*, design-level form — it is not pipeline leakage and must not be conflated with it. Tag `design-level-oracle`, not `oracle-leak`.
prospective: **no** — retrospective throughout. Every protein comes from an already-deposited PDB/CATH/PISCES set (p15–16); the models are pre-trained checkpoints; nothing is predicted ahead of an unknown answer and nothing is tested experimentally. The axis is partly ill-fitting: this paper makes no structural predictions to be prospective *about*. Its interventional design does mean the *effects* are not cherry-picked post hoc from an observational sweep, but the expected direction of every effect was declared in advance (route 7).
state_metric: **DUAL — binary predicate + continuous coordinate.** (a) **Binary predicate**, fully operationalised with stated thresholds, App E p15: hairpin = DSSP E/B, each strand ≥2 residues, connecting loop 0–5 residues, strands sequentially adjacent; helix-loop-helix = DSSP H, each helix ≥4 residues, loop 2–8 residues, helices sequentially adjacent. Justification of the thresholds is **NOT REPORTED** — they are asserted, not derived or sensitivity-tested. (b) **Continuous coordinates** used alongside: mean cross-strand Cα distance in Å (p6, p22), mean pairwise Cα distance in Å (p7, p23), interpolation coefficient α of `z` toward the donor (Eq. 3, p4), probe R² and ROC-AUC (p7, p20–21, p23). No `visual-metric` call anywhere — even the structure renders (Fig 18, p23) are backed by the quantified dose–response of Fig 17.
metric_saturation: **Yes, numerically, in two places, and both are acknowledged by the authors.** (1) **Charge steering dose–response saturates**, verbatim p22 (Fig 17 caption): "All three models show effects emerging above a threshold around 0.4 std-DoM units and **saturating thereafter**, indicating that charge functions as a continuous biochemical signal…" — so the reported α = 3σ operating point sits far into the saturated regime, and effect sizes reported at α = 3σ are ceiling values, not slopes. (2) **Charge-direction ROC-AUC ceilings**: ESMFold and OpenFold "rise to near 1.0 within the first 5–10 blocks" and stay there for the rest of the trunk (p21), so that curve carries no information about blocks 10–47. Non-saturating: patching success rates (max ≈62.5%, p17), Procrustes R² (plateau ≈0.9), CKA (max ≈0.9). Figure-level obscuring is recorded in `hides`, not here.
directional_control: **Yes — the paper's whole point is that the output motif can be instructed, and it names four independent handles.** (1) **Donor activation at a chosen block** — sequence patch in blocks 0–7 or pairwise patch in blocks 25–40 sets which motif appears; the reverse direction (helix donor into hairpin target) works too: "The reverse setup (helix donor, hairpin target) is identical with motif roles swapped" (p3) and "The two-stage structure holds for both hairpin and helix induction" (p9). (2) **Charge direction with per-strand sign** — `s'ᵢ = sᵢ + αv_charge` on one flank and `− αv_charge` on the other induces hairpins; same-sign on both flanks pushes strands apart (p6). (3) **Distance-probe weight direction with sign and target distance** — steering `z` toward 5.5 Å pulls cross-strand pairs into contact (p8). (4) **Scalar magnitude of `z` before the structure module** — expands or contracts the whole predicted structure monotonically (p7, p23). None of these is a conformational-state handle in the corpus's sense (no partner, ligand, nanobody, template or MSA manipulation is used anywhere).
anti_memorization_design: **NONE.** There is no post-cutoff set, no date-based holdout, and no training-cutoff discussion for any of the three models. Model training cutoffs are never stated. What *does* exist is ordinary train/test hygiene for the probes, which is a different thing: 400 training / 200 evaluation proteins for the distance probes (p7); a probing test set of held-out hairpins disjoint from the training hairpins; and, verbatim p16, "Hairpin sequences were further filtered to ensure ≤ 25% pairwise sequence identity to any α-helical sequence or previously selected hairpin, and to exclude exact matches to donor sequences used in activation patching." That guards against probe overfitting and donor/target overlap, not against the models having memorised the PDB.
anti_memorization_control: **NONE RUN.** No arm of this paper tests whether the effects survive on structures the models cannot have seen. Given that the entire dataset is X-ray PDB entries culled up to 2025-02-19 (p16), essentially every protein used is plausibly in-training for all three models. Whether the two-stage structure would appear on post-cutoff or synthetic sequences is untested and unmentioned.
confidence_as_discriminator: **No — pLDDT is never used to judge correctness, and this is deliberate.** Success is DSSP-based throughout (App E, p15). pLDDT appears exactly once, as a limitation on the *products* of the interventions, verbatim p14: "The counterfactual structures we produce show low pLDDT, and inverse folding fails to recover sequences that fold to these structures. Interventions can also create unrealistic proteins with steric clashes or chain breaks." No pTM, ipTM, or confidence filtering anywhere. Not tagged `confidence-as-discriminator`. **Read this carefully before citing the paper for transferable interventions: the intervention reliably changes the motif DSSP reports, and reliably produces a structure the model itself is not confident in.**
stance: **`precedent` on findings + `contrast` on rigour** (provisional; the user's call). **Precedent**: it is the closest thing in the corpus to a direct demonstration that a trunk-level activation intervention localises to the same block window across models and that a pairwise-track representation from one model can be linearly mapped into another and still do its job — exactly the load-bearing premise for cross-model trunk interventions. **Contrast**: the convergence claim is made across three AlphaFold-lineage trunks with no untrained/architecture-matched null and no non-AF architecture; cross-model patching succeeds at only 10–17%; and the intervention's outputs are explicitly low-pLDDT and not sequence-realisable, so "the intervention transfers" is true at the representation level and unproven at the level of usable structures.
n_predictions: **Samples per target**: 10 donors sampled per motif per target (p3). **Targets**: 200 for patching (100 helical + 100 hairpin, p16). **Total**: "yielding ≈10,000 patching experiments" (p3), of which "Approximately 40% of patches (≈4,000 cases) successfully produce the donor motif" (p3); the detailed flow analysis uses "400 successful cases of block-0 sequence patching" (p4). Other totals: ~500 steering cases per model (p6); 500 sampled β-hairpins for same-charge steering (p6); 600 proteins for structure-module scaling (p7); 400 train / 200 eval for distance probes (p7). All three models receive the same sweeps (p14). Compute: ~1,000–1,500 GPU-hours, 2–3 weeks wall-clock on 2× RTX A6000 (p15).
si_in_scope: **SI HELD** — Appendices A–M (pp13–28) and the NeurIPS checklist (pp29–35) are all inside this 35-page PDF; there is no external supplement. **But note a distinct gap: the paper contains no numeric results table at all.** The only table is Table 1 (p15), which reports wall-clock times. Every quantitative result below is either an approximate value stated in prose (with the authors' own "≈", "around", "near" hedges) or read off a figure axis; per-model, per-block values are not tabulated anywhere and cannot be recovered from the PDF.

title: Investigating whether deep learning models for co-folding learn the physics of protein-ligand interactions
system: **General protein-ligand, with two protein kinases as the named case studies.** - Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2), PDB 1B38, with ATP — protein kinase (p.2, p.9). - MEK1, PDB 7XLP, with an ATP-site inhibitor — protein kinase (p.3, p.9). - Glucose dehydrogenase, PDB 2VWH, with glucose — general protein (p.5, p.9). - CASF-2016, 285 experimentally-determined protein-ligand complexes, taxonomically unrestricted (p.4, p.9). Three further binding-site mutagenesis systems are run on AF3 in SI Fig. S17 (p.9) — identities not given in the main PDF.
n_targets: **288 protein-ligand systems in total**: 3 hand-picked case studies (CDK2/ATP, MEK1/inhibitor, glucose dehydrogenase/glucose) + 285 CASF-2016 complexes (p.9), plus 3 unnamed SI systems (p.9). The four-model head-to-head comparison runs on the **3 case studies only**; the systematic 285-complex sweep is **AlphaFold3 only** — "Structures were predicted using only the AlphaFold3 co-folding model and the highest-confidence structure was used for analysis." (p.9). The generality claim ("to further confirm this behavior as a widespread issue for protein-ligand structure predictions", p.4) therefore rests on one backbone at scale and four backbones on three systems.
method_class: **benchmark-only (adversarial robustness benchmark of co-folding models) + enhanced sampling (funnel metadynamics) as the orthogonal physics control.** No new predictor is proposed. Verbatim framing, p.8 Methods: "In this study, we perform several types of adversarial challenges by crafting examples with an expected physical outcome and seeing if the predictions from co-folding models agree with this expectation."
backbones: **Four, head to head — AlphaFold3, RoseTTAFold All-Atom (RFAA), Chai-1, Boltz-1** (p.9). → `multi-backbone`. Note the CASF-2016 sweep drops to **AlphaFold3 only** (p.9). Versions are not stated for any of the four; no commit hashes, no dates. Run conditions: "Unless otherwise noted, each models was run using default settings and no constraints were specified to the models that support this feature." (p.9) — i.e. **no pocket constraint was used**, even where the model supports one.
templates: **ON (by default), and templates are the paper's own explanation for the failure.** No explicit "templates on" sentence exists; it follows from default settings (p.9) plus the mechanistic account on pp.7–8: > "Most of the co-folding models rely heavily on multiple-sequence alignment and 3D template-based input features retrieved from existing data which help the model predict the 3D structure. However, when we introduce small mutations, for example by removing the binding site, it is very likely that the sequence alignment and template search will return exactly the same results as before, as they are still the closest related sequences and structures in the dataset. Therefore, the MSA and template features that the network accepts as input are identical despite the mutations, leading the model to produce a very similar prediction." (pp.7–8) → tag `templates-on`. **Not** state-annotated; no template curation of any kind is performed by the authors.
msa_handling: **full** (default settings, p.9). Never subsampled, never clustered, never state-filtered. The MSA is load-bearing in the *diagnosis*: the mutated sequence retrieves the same alignment as the wild type, so the pocket perturbation never reaches the network's evolutionary features (pp.7–8, quoted above).
states_generated: **one** — a single predicted protein-ligand complex per (model × input condition). For the CASF sweep an internal sample is reduced to one by confidence: "the highest-confidence structure was used for analysis" (p.9). The number of seeds / diffusion samples generated before that selection is **NOT REPORTED** anywhere in the main text or Methods. `NOT APPLICABLE` as a *conformational* state count — nothing multi-state is generated or sought.
structural_priors_used: **Heavy, deliberate, and not a defect** — the entire design is built on deposited co-crystal structures. - Three co-crystal complexes are the starting scaffolds and the references: CDK2 PDB 1B38, MEK1 PDB 7XLP, glucose dehydrogenase PDB 2VWH (pp.9–10). - The perturbation sites are read off the crystal contacts: "Residues with side-chain heavy atoms within 3.5 Å of any ligand heavy atoms were selected for mutation." (p.9), and for the sweep, "Binding site residues were identified with the co-crystallized ligand using the same distance threshold of 3.5 Å." (p.9). The explicit CDK2 list is I10, T14, V18, A31, K33, D86, K129, Q131, N132, L134, D145; the MEK1 list is A40, A59, I105, E108, M110, S158, F173 (p.9). - CASF-2016 (285 high-quality experimental complexes, ref. 53) is used as the evaluation corpus (p.9). - The funnel-metadynamics funnel is placed on the crystallographic pocket: "funnel metadynamics simulations were set up so that the ligand is initially placed at the start of a funnel encompassing the full binding site" (p.10). - Systems were chosen *because* their PDB representation is known: ATP "is widely represented in the PDB training data" (p.9); glucose because "sugar structures are widely represented in the PDB training data" (p.9). - The mutation table itself is a prior from the literature, not from structures: the Miyata distance (ref. 52), tabulated in Table 2, p.9.
oracle_leakage: **Present by three of seven routes. Critically, the leakage that matters here is leakage *into the models under test*, which the authors deliberately preserve and then name as the mechanism of failure — it is the paper's finding, not the paper's sin.** Enumerated route by route. **Route 1 — deposited structures as input or template: PRESENT, and it is the central result.** Models run at default settings retrieve MSA and template features for the *wild-type* sequence even when every contacting residue has been mutated, so a deposited structure of the unperturbed complex re-enters the pipeline through template search. Verbatim, pp.7–8: > "when we introduce small mutations, for example by removing the binding site, it is very likely that the sequence alignment and template search will return exactly the same results as before, as they are still the closest related sequences and structures in the dataset. Therefore, the MSA and template features that the network accepts as input are identical despite the mutations, leading the model to produce a very similar prediction." Compounded by training-set membership, stated outright, p.3: > "The CDK2-ATP complex was part of the training set used to develop the co-folding methods." Note the authors never run a templates-off arm to isolate this route — the mechanism is asserted and argued, not measured. That is the single largest hole in the paper. **Route 2 — state annotations from a curated database (GPCRdb / KLIFS / Kincore) driving templates or alignments: NONE FOUND.** No such database appears anywhere. Protocol described p.9 (Methods, "Binding site mutations", "CASF-2016 dataset") and p.10 ("Ligand mutations"): binding-site residues come from a 3.5 Å distance criterion on the co-crystallised ligand, and mutations come from the Miyata volume/polarity distance (Table 2, p.9). Nothing state-annotated. **Route 3 — cluster labels derived from known states: NONE FOUND.** No clustering drives any prediction. The one grouping performed is a *post hoc* analysis of results, not an input: "we investigated whether belonging to particular protein families played a significant role by grouping results from the CASF predictions into their protein families. These results... show no clear separation between protein families that perform robustly or not." (p.8) **Route 4 — hyperparameters, sweep ranges, seeds or stopping criteria tuned against known states: essentially NONE FOUND, with one recorded exception.** Default settings throughout: "Unless otherwise noted, each models was run using default settings and no constraints were specified to the models that support this feature." (p.9). No sweep range is tuned on the evaluation set; the funnel-metadynamics parameters are explicitly held fixed across targets: "For each protein target, the funnel parameters were kept the same" (p.10). The exception is a single abandoned rescue attempt made against a known reference, p.3: > "Additional attempts at rescuing RFAA accuracy by increasing the maximum number of cycles did not improve results." This is per-system tuning aimed at a held reference; it is reported as having failed, and no tuned value is carried forward, so it does not contaminate the reported numbers — but it is the correct home for it. **Route 5 — success defined post hoc by RMSD to a structure they had: PRESENT, and unavoidable by construction.** The whole readout is RMSD to a deposited pose. Verbatim, p.4: > "Irrespective of the type of modification, more than half of all systems correctly predicted by AlphaFold3 (ligand RMSD < 2 Å) retain the same predicted ligand pose even after binding site disruption." And in the simulation control, p.10: > "The bound state was defined by having RMSD < 2 Å to the native pose, all other stable states outside of the pocket are considered to be unbound." This is a *benign* instance of route 5: the reference pose is the object of the test, not a hidden answer key — the perturbed systems have no experimental structure at all, so no other reference exists. The consequence is recorded under `metric_saturation` and `hides` instead. **Route 6 — best/worst model labels assigned against a held reference: NONE FOUND.** Selection is by the model's own confidence, not by the reference: "the highest-confidence structure was used for analysis" (p.9). No best-of-N against RMSD anywhere. For the case-study figures, the number of predictions generated per cell and how one was chosen for display is **NOT REPORTED** (Figs. 1, 2, 4, 5 captions, pp.3, 4, 6, 7) — which is a reporting gap, not evidence of reference-based selection. **Route 7 — design-level oracle use (weaker than pipeline leakage; label kept distinct): PRESENT and explicit.** The expected answer is declared before the result is read, as a matter of stated method, p.8: > "In this study, we perform several types of adversarial challenges by crafting examples with an expected physical outcome and seeing if the predictions from co-folding models agree with this expectation." Systems are chosen because their training-set status is known in advance — ATP/CDK2 because it *is* in training ("ATP is a good test case since it is widely represented in the PDB training data", p.9; "The CDK2-ATP complex was part of the training set used to develop the co-folding methods", p.3), MEK1 because it is *not* ("MEK1 was selected as an additional test case since it was not included in the training set of any of the tested co-folding models and has low similarity in terms of ligand and pocket shape.", p.9). The expected outcomes are asserted a priori: "Methylation of glucose can be assumed to result in non-binders that lose all affinity to the target" (pp.9–10); "the assumption is that such a strong difference in charge should show a significantly different binding mode of at least the charged groups, if not complete loss of binding" (p.10). **Mitigating and important:** the a priori expectation is subsequently tested independently by funnel metadynamics (Table 1, p.8) rather than merely asserted — which is precisely the control that converts route 7 from a defect into a validated prior. → tags `oracle-leak` *and* `design-level-oracle`.
prospective: **no.** Every arm is scored against a deposited co-crystal pose, and the perturbed systems are synthetic constructs with no experimental structure and no experimental binding data. There is no wet-lab measurement anywhere in the paper. The nearest thing to a prospective element is design-level: MEK1 is a genuine out-of-training-set target (p.9), and the perturbed pockets are novel inputs no model has seen — but the *ground truth* for those inputs is a simulation (funnel metadynamics), not an experiment. Authors' own framing agrees: "additional validation such as physics-based methods, such as molecular dynamics simulations or free energy calculations, or experimental data may be necessary." (p.8, recommending experiment as future work).
state_metric: **Triple, and deliberately not a conformational-state metric — it is ligand pose correctness under perturbation.** Joined: **binary predicate + RMSD-to-reference + visual only.** 1. **Binary predicate**: ligand heavy-atom RMSD < 2 Å to the native co-crystal pose. Used for the CASF sweep readout ("more than half of all systems correctly predicted by AlphaFold3 (ligand RMSD < 2 Å)", p.4; Fig. 3 y-axis "Fraction with RMSD < 2Å to Native Pose", p.5) and to define the bound state in the simulations ("The bound state was defined by having RMSD < 2 Å to the native pose", p.10). **Threshold justification: NOT REPORTED** — 2 Å is used as convention (it is the same threshold quoted for the PoseBusters V2 comparison on p.2) and is never argued for. 2. **RMSD-to-reference, continuous**: individual values are quoted in prose for the CDK2 case study only — AF3 0.2 Å, RFAA 2.2 Å wild-type, RFAA 2.0 Å after binding-site removal (p.2). No continuous RMSD distribution is ever plotted. 3. **Visual only**: the dominant readout for Figs. 1, 2, 4 and 5 — pose displacement, steric clashes and stretched bonds are called by eye from renders with no quantitative panel. E.g. "There are also instances of unphysical overlapping atoms and large steric clashes in several of the predicted structures" (p.3); "Several steric clashes and stretched bonds were observed between the ligand, co-factor, and protein in the RFAA predictions with the addition of methyls." (p.5); "No obvious steric clashes or non-physical artifacts were observed in the wild-type predicted structures." (p.5). No clash count, no interaction-energy number, no distance cutoff is given for any of these calls. → tag `visual-metric`, and this is a real rigour defect in a paper whose headline is about physical validity. **RMSD atom-selection caveat (matters):** for the modified-ligand arms, RMSD is computed over corresponding heavy atoms only — "in the methylation challenge, only the original heavy atoms of the sugar contribute to the RMSD, not the additional methyl groups. In the charge modification example, the charged groups were included in the RMSD calculation." (p.10). So the methylation series is scored on a sub-structure that the perturbation deliberately does not touch, which mechanically biases that arm's RMSD downward.
metric_saturation: **Yes, numerically, in two places — and the direction matters differently in each.** 1. **Funnel-metadynamics probabilities floor and ceiling hard (Table 1, p.8).** Bound-state probability hits exactly `0.00 ± 0.00` (unbound `1.00 ± 0.00`) for: binding-site packing, binding-site inversion, glucose with 3/4/5/6 methyls, and ATP at charge +1, +2 and +3 — 11 of the 15 tabulated rows. Below "no binding at all" the metric has no resolution, so the perturbations **cannot be rank-ordered by severity** past that point. Here the saturation **is the finding**: it is the positive evidence that the perturbed pockets are genuinely unbindable, which is what makes the co-folding models' unchanged poses indefensible. It is not an artefact — but it does mean the paper cannot say which of packing, inversion or charge reversal is the harsher challenge. 2. **The RMSD < 2 Å predicate floors the pose readout.** Fig. 3 (p.5) reports only the *fraction* below 2 Å; the underlying RMSD distribution is never shown, so "unchanged pose" and "shifted 1.9 Å" are indistinguishable in every reported number. Combined with the methylation-arm atom selection (original heavy atoms only, p.10) this makes low RMSD **partly an artefact of the metric** in the ligand-modification arms specifically. In the binding-site mutagenesis arms the low RMSD is not an artefact — the renders (Figs. 1, 2, pp.3–4) show the ligand sitting in the same place, and the funnel metadynamics independently shows it should not be there at all. **Verdict: floored, and the floor is load-bearing evidence rather than a defect — with one genuine artefact confined to the glucose methylation series.** Axis-related issues are recorded in `hides` (Fig. 3 row), not here, per v3 rule 9.
directional_control: **The handle exists and is exactly what the paper shows does not work.** The intended handle is not a state selector but a *physical* one: mutate the pocket (Gly removal / Phe packing / Miyata inversion, p.9) or chemically modify the ligand (progressive methylation, charge reversal −3 → 0/+1/+2/+3, pp.9–10) and the ligand should move. It does not. No other handle is used: no pocket constraint, despite availability — "no constraints were specified to the models that support this feature" (p.9); no template bias, no MSA manipulation, no seed steering, no partner or nanobody. The paper also notes the models are in principle unconstrained yet behave as if constrained, p.5: > "It should be noted that in contrast to classical docking methods where the binding pose is typically limited to a predefined search volume, co-folding methods are in principle able to place the ligand anywhere on the protein surface. However, each of the tested co-folding models demonstrated a specific bias towards a given pocket rather than exploring other, potentially unspecific binding modes on the surface."
anti_memorization_design: **Yes, but n = 1 and no date cutoff.** One out-of-training-set system was deliberately selected: > "MEK1 was selected as an additional test case since it was not included in the training set of any of the tested co-folding models and has low similarity in terms of ligand and pocket shape. The system was identified via the Runs N' Poses dataset (ref. 49) which calculated a similarity value (sucos_shape_pocket_qcov) of 46.21." (p.9) The cutoff is defined by **membership in the tested models' training sets** (via an external curated dataset) plus a **pocket/ligand shape-similarity score**, not by a deposition date. n = 1 protein (PDB 7XLP). CASF-2016 is **not** a held-out set — it predates the models' training and is expected to be largely inside it. No post-cutoff set exists anywhere in the paper.
anti_memorization_control: **RUN, and UNPOWERED (n = 1).** The MEK1 arm is not merely declared — it is executed as a full parallel challenge battery (wild type, removal, packing, inversion × 4 models) and analysed in its own figure (Fig. 2, p.4) and its own paragraph (pp.3–4). The result is that memorisation of *that specific complex* is not required for the failure: "The trend continues in the binding site packing challenge where we again observe near-native poses without any significant deviation despite the dramatic changes to the pocket." (p.3). Mark **UNPOWERED**: one protein, one ligand, no statistics, and RFAA fails even on the unperturbed wild type ("with RFAA still placing near the binding site, but failing to retrieve a near-native pose", p.3), which removes one of the four models from that arm's evidence. A second, indirect anti-memorisation control was run at scale on CASF and reported as null: "no correlation between the number of examples in the training set versus model sensitivity against adversarial changes was observed." (p.8) — n = 285, but with the number itself and the correlation coefficient in SI, not in the PDF.
confidence_as_discriminator: **Yes — used, and explicitly validated as a *failure*.** Ligand pLDDT, ligand pTM and protein-ligand ipTM are recorded for every case system (SI Tables S1–S4, pp.4, 5) and mean ligand pLDDT is the stratifying variable of Fig. 3. The tested question is whether high confidence separates the physically indefensible predictions from the sound ones; it does not: > "This proportion of conserved binding modes is largely independent of the confidence score. For example, among complexes with a confidence score > 80, between 42% and 52% maintain an unaltered ligand pose depending on the disruption applied (compared to 78% unaltered in the absence of disruption)." (p.4) > "they can generate non-physical, high-energy structures with considerable confidence." (p.8) The interpretive caveat is stated by the authors themselves: "While it remains to be determined exactly how to interpret these values in the context of individual atoms rather than protein residues, the same general trend appears to hold: scores above 70 indicate high confidence, and scores above 90 reflect very high confidence." (p.4). → tag `confidence-as-discriminator`; this is one of the cleanest negative validations of confidence-as-discriminator in the corpus.
stance: **PROVISIONAL — user's call.** `contrast (on rigour) + threat`.
n_predictions: - **Samples per target: NOT REPORTED.** The number of seeds or diffusion samples generated per input is never stated for any model. For CASF the existence of multiple samples is implied only by "the highest-confidence structure was used for analysis" (p.9); the pool size is not given. - **Targets**: 3 case-study systems (4 models each) + 285 CASF-2016 complexes (AF3 only) + 3 unnamed SI systems (AF3 only). - **Distinct input conditions, computable from the text/figures**: CDK2 mutagenesis 4 conditions × 4 models = 16 (Fig. 1, p.3); MEK1 mutagenesis 4 × 4 = 16 (Fig. 2, p.4); glucose methylation 6 states × 4 models = 24 (Fig. 4, p.6); ATP charge 6 variants × 4 models = 24 (Fig. 5B–C, p.7); CASF 4 conditions × 285 × AF3 = 1140 (p.9). **≈ 1220 displayed/analysed predictions**, each of unknown internal sample count. Plus an apo arm over the mutated CASF proteins (p.8), size not stated. - **Simulations**: 15 tabulated systems × 3 replicates × 1000 ns = **45 μs of funnel metadynamics** (p.8 Table 1, p.10).
si_in_scope: **SI NOT HELD — and a substantial fraction of the quantitative content lives there.** The 12-page PDF contains only Table 1 and Fig. 3 as quantitative displays. Absent from the corpus: Figs. S1–S2 (2D/3D interaction diagrams for the mutated CDK2/MEK1 structures, p.4); Tables S1–S2 (ligand pLDDT, ligand pTM, protein-ligand ipTM for CDK2 and MEK1, p.4); Figs. S3–S4 (interaction diagrams, sugar and charge modifications, p.5); Tables S3–S4 (confidence metrics for those two systems, p.5); Table S5 (Tanimoto similarities of every modified ligand, p.5); Figs. S5–S6 (ligand RMSD time evolution for every funnel MD run, p.6); Figs. S7–S12 (per-system performance across the three challenges vs. ligand pLDDT, p.8); Figs. S13–S14 (protein-family breakdown of CASF results, p.8); Fig. S15 (physicochemical property analysis, p.8); Fig. S16 (apo vs holo CASF, p.8); Fig. S17 (three additional AF3 mutagenesis systems, p.9). **Every per-system number and every confidence value is in SI.** Predicted structures are on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo record 14749304, p.10); code on Zenodo record 14768184 under MIT licence (p.10).

year: 2023. Received 30 September 2022; accepted 10 July 2023 (p.1).
venue: *Nature Communications* 14:4361. **Peer-reviewed, not a preprint** — "Peer review information Nature Communications thanks Andreas Bock, Roland Dunbrack and the other, anonymous, reviewer(s) for their contribution to the peer review of this work. A peer review file is available." (p.17). → tag `peer-reviewed`.
title: GPCRome-wide analysis of G-protein-coupling diversity using a computational biology approach
system: **GPCR**, specifically GPCR–heterotrimeric G-protein complexes and their intracellular coupling interface. Receptor classes A, B1, B2, C and Frizzled (p.2). Nine Gα proteins in the experimental set: GNAS, GNAI1, GNAI2, GNAI3, GNAT1, GNAO1, GNAQ, GNA11, GNA13 (p.2). One receptor, CCKAR, is taken into wet-lab validation (p.4, p.14).
n_targets: **Four distinct counts; do not collapse them.** - *Experimental structural set*: 376 PDB entries met the Pfam criterion, 362 retained after excluding chimeras (p.12), comprising **166 Gs, 184 Gi/o, 9 Gq/11 and 3 G12/13** complexes and "corresponding to 93, 17, 10, 3, and 2 unique receptors from Class A, B1, B2, C and Frizzled, respectively, and entailing 9 different G-proteins" (p.2). - *Non-redundant representative set*: **125** GPCR–G-protein pairs, one representative per receptor–G-protein pair chosen by resolution then sequence coverage (p.2, p.13); Fig. 1C breaks these into 73 Gi/o, 43 Gs, 6 Gq/11, 3 G12/13 (p.3). - *AlphaFold benchmark*: the same **125** complexes, predicted twice (with and without templates) (p.7, p.13). - *GPCRome-wide prediction set*: **996 GPCR–Gα pairs**, "reported to bind in UCM33 ... respectively corresponding to 164 and 13 human GPCRs and Gα proteins (the three members of the transducin family were not considered)" (p.13), filtered down to **825** complexes for analysis (p.8, p.13). The generality claim is "GPCRome-wide" but the modelled space is 164 of ~800 human GPCRs and only pairs already reported to couple — see `oracle_leakage` route 7.
method_class: **Compound — co-folding + benchmark-only + other (structural bioinformatics of interfaces, Rosetta multistate design, Rosetta interface energetics).** No new predictor is built. AlphaFold-Multimer is used off the shelf, benchmarked against 125 experimental complexes, then run at scale; the primary analysis is interface contact-network and fingerprint bioinformatics on both experimental and predicted complexes; a Rosetta multistate design arm produces mutants that are then tested in cells.
backbones: **AlphaFold-Multimer v2.3.1 only** (p.13: "We used Alphafold-Multimer v2.3.1 to generate 3D models of GPCR-heterotrimeric G-protein complexes."). Single backbone — **not** `multi-backbone`. Non-AF structural tooling: Rosetta relax, RosettaDock (`docking_local_refine`), Rosetta InterfaceAnalyzer and Rosetta multistate design, all from RosettaCommons version 2021.16.61629 (p.14, p.15).
templates: **DUAL — on for the production run, off in one benchmark ablation arm.** Verbatim, p.13: > "We generated 3D models 'using templates', that is allowing AlphaFold-Multimer to use the 3D structural models available in the PDB (they are used only to predict the structure of single chains), and 'without templates', running the predictions setting --max_template_date=01-01-1900 instead, to avoid the usage of any available experimental template." Production GPCRome run is templates-on: "We, therefore, ran multimer predictions with available templates for receptor-heterotrimeric G-protein complexes whose receptor-α subunit binary interactions are reported in the UCM dataset." (p.7). **Important qualifier the authors state themselves: templates are monomer-only** — "(they are used only to predict the structure of single chains)" (p.13), so the *interface* is never templated even in the templates-on arm. Templates are **not** state-annotated or curated in any way; no template date cutoff other than the 1900 ablation. → tag `templates-on`.
msa_handling: **full (default AlphaFold-Multimer pipeline).** The words "MSA", "multiple sequence alignment", "subsampl", "cluster the alignment" and "seed" never appear anywhere in the paper in connection with the AF runs; the only MSA-relevant sentence is "The databases required to run AlphaFold-Multimer were downloaded on 12 January 2023." (p.13). No subsampling, no clustering, no state-filtering, no pinning is described. Recorded as full-by-default, with the caveat that the paper never states it.
states_generated: **one.** Five AF-Multimer models are generated per complex and exactly one is kept, selected by AlphaFold's own ranking score, never by any state criterion — p.13: "Among the 5 models generated for each GPCR-G-protein complex, only the best one was considered for further analysis. The score used to evaluate the models was the default one used by AlphaFold-Multimer (0.2*pTM + 0.8*ipTM)." No ensemble is retained, no alternative state is sought, no comparison of alternative receptor conformations appears anywhere. The experimental-structure arm generates nothing (it analyses deposited PDB entries).
structural_priors_used: **Extensive, deliberate, and mostly not a defect.** - The 362 deposited GPCR–G-protein complexes are the reference corpus, retrieved via SIFTS/Pfam mapping (p.12). - The 125 non-redundant representatives are the benchmark reference set (p.2, p.13). - GPCRdb generic numbering (ref. 31) and the Common G-protein Numbering scheme (ref. 32) provide the residue coordinate system for all contact analysis: "We then mapped contacting residues to consensus numbering through GPCRdb31 (Supplementary Data 2) and the common G-protein numbering (CGN)32 schemes" (p.2). These are **numbering** schemes here, not state annotations. - The RMSD/RMSF superposition frame is defined from what is solved in every structure: "We considered 141 GPCR and 73 G-protein consensus positions defining respectively the consensus core of the 7TM domain and the Ras GTPase domain solved in all experimental structures." (p.15); RMSF references are the group centroids, PDB 8E3X (Gs) and 8F7S (Gi/o) (p.15). - The multistate design starts from solved complexes of the same receptor in two coupling states: "As a starting template for the design, we have chosen CCKAR (UniProt Accession: P32238), a cholecystokinin receptor that has been solved in complex with Gs (PDB ID: 7EZK), Gi/o (PDB ID: 7EZH") and Gq/11 (PDB ID: 7EZM)52." (p.14). Positive and negative design states are literally these two PDB entries: "Next, we designated positive state and negative state complexes (7ezk or 7ezh)." (p.14). - Coupling labels are priors too, taken from the Universal/Common Coupling Map (UCM, ref. 33) and from GEMTA / Shedding / GtoPDB (Fig. 3 caption, p.5).
oracle_leakage: **Present on five of seven routes; clean on two. All of it is oracle knowledge about the *interface / coupling label*, none of it about a *receptor conformational state*, because the paper never defines a receptor state to leak.** **Route 1 — deposited structures used as input or template: PRESENT.** The production GPCRome run is templates-on with no date cutoff, so a receptor whose active-state monomer is deposited gets that monomer as a template. p.7: "We, therefore, ran multimer predictions with available templates for receptor-heterotrimeric G-protein complexes whose receptor-α subunit binary interactions are reported in the UCM dataset." And the same applies to the 125-complex benchmark templates-on arm, where the reference structure's own monomers are in the template database. **Mitigation, stated by the authors:** templates act on single chains only — "(they are used only to predict the structure of single chains)" (p.13) — and the ablation arm shows the interface accuracy barely depends on them (DockQ 0.664 vs 0.645, p.7). **Route 2 — state annotations from a curated database driving templates or alignments: NONE FOUND.** GPCRdb is used, but only as a residue-numbering scheme for contact mapping and for the snake-plot rendering in Fig. 5D (p.2, p.8, p.13); it never selects templates and never modifies an alignment. Protocol described p.12–p.13 ("Data sets", "GPCR-Gα complexes prediction via AlphaFold-Multimer") — the only inputs named are sequences, and the only template control is the `--max_template_date` flag. No KLIFS/Kincore analogue and no GPCRdb state annotation (active/inactive) is used anywhere. **Route 3 — cluster labels derived from known states: PRESENT, in the form of coupling labels rather than conformational states, and it is upstream of an analysis the paper calls "unsupervised".** The contacts fed to the fingerprint clustering are pre-selected using experimentally known coupling labels via a log-odds ratio computed over "coupled / not coupled" contingency counts. p.2: > "We also estimated the contact positions that are more frequent than expected in each coupling group through log-odds ratio statistics (see Methods), and we used this information to filter the most informative contacts for Gs and Gi/o couplings (Fig. 3). CF clustering identifies two main clusters: the largest one (cluster 1), is enriched with Gs complexes ... The second cluster (i.e. cluster 2), is enriched almost exclusively with Gi/o complexes" The LOR itself is label-driven, p.14: "CC and CN terms represent the number of GPCRs coupled to a specific Gprotein group (Gi/o or Gs) that are or are not, respectively, in contact at that position". Filter thresholds are stated in the Fig. 3 caption (p.5): "Only contacts present in at least 10% of the structures and having an absolute LOR value greater than 2 are considered." **Mitigating control the authors run:** the unfiltered clustering is also reported and gives a different answer — "When relaxing the criteria to perform CF clustering by removing the log-odds ratio filter and by including all unique complexes, the clustering is now mainly guided by the receptor class" (p.2, Supplementary Fig. 2). That control is exactly the right one and it shows the Gs/Gi split in Fig. 3 is partly a product of the label-driven filter. **Route 4 — hyperparameters, sweep ranges or stopping criteria tuned against known states: PRESENT, twice, and both are thresholds read directly off the reference structures.** p.13, verbatim: > "we kept only models with ΔSASA ≥ 1500 Å2, which is slightly less than the minimum ΔSASA found in all experimental structures. In this way we removed 32 more structures" and > "We removed 21 predicted complexes (975 structures left) based on unrealistic complex topologies, i.e. not having any of the following G-protein's H5 positions, i.e. H5.16, H5.19, H5.20, H5.23, H5.24, H5.25, that we found to most recurrently mediate contacts with GPCR's residues in experimental structures." Both filters are calibrated on the experimental complexes and then applied to the predicted ones, which is leakage of the reference set into the composition of the analysed prediction set. The third filter, pDockQ ≥ 0.23, is taken from the literature and not tuned here: "We kept only the structures with pDockQ ≥ 0.2348 (118 out of 975 structures removed)36." (p.13). Note also that the pLDDT < 70 residue-trimming threshold is asserted, not justified against anything (p.13). **Route 5 — success defined post hoc by RMSD/DockQ to a structure they had: PRESENT and unavoidable by construction.** The entire AF benchmark is scored against the 125 deposited complexes. p.7: > "We first benchmarked AF-multimer by assessing the prediction performances with or without 3D templates for 125 representative GPCR-G-protein complexes with available experimental structures. Using 3D templates in the prediction slightly improves the performances, assessed by measuring the deviation of predicted vs. experimental interfaces via either the DockQ metric (Wilcoxon P = 0.021; Fig. 9A) or the fraction of native contacts (Wilcoxon P = 0.004; Fig. 9B)." The composite filter is itself justified against the same reference: "Such a filtering scheme improves the correlation between prediction scores (pDockQ) and distance from experimental structures (DockQ) in the benchmark (Fig. 9C, D)." (p.7). This is a benign, disclosed instance — the reference is the object of the benchmark — but it is route 5. **Route 6 — best/worst model labels assigned against a held reference: NONE FOUND.** Model selection is by AlphaFold's own confidence, never against the reference. Protocol, p.13: "Among the 5 models generated for each GPCR-G-protein complex, only the best one was considered for further analysis. The score used to evaluate the models was the default one used by AlphaFold-Multimer (0.2*pTM + 0.8*ipTM)." No best-of-N-by-DockQ appears anywhere. **Route 7 — design-level oracle use (weaker than pipeline leakage; kept distinct): PRESENT and explicit, on both the prediction and the design arms.** - The prediction set is defined by pairs whose answer is already known to be "they couple": "A total of 996 GPCR-Gɑ pairs, reported to bind in UCM33, were considered" (p.13); "we predicted through AlphaFold-multimer (v2.3)37 996 GPCR - G-protein alpha subunit pairs from UCM binary interactions" (p.7). No non-coupling pair is modelled as a negative control, so the pipeline is never asked to fail. - The wet-lab target is chosen because both answers are deposited: CCKAR "has been solved in complex with both Gs (PDB ID: 7EZK) and Gi/o (PDB ID: 7EZH)" (p.4). - The expected direction of the designed mutations is declared before assay: "in one hand we sought to retain Gs while removing Gi/o couplings, and on the other, we maintained Gi/o while reducing binding to Gs" (p.4). This one is mitigated — the prediction is then tested in cells and mostly fails (5 of 8 mutations had no effect, p.5), which is the honest outcome. → tags `oracle-leak` and `design-level-oracle`.
prospective: **partial.** *Retrospective* in the prediction pipeline: every accuracy number is scored against structures the authors already had, the model-filtering thresholds are calibrated on those structures, and the modelled pairs are pairs already reported to couple. *Prospective* in one arm only: the eight designed CCKAR mutants are new sequences with no prior structure or assay, tested blind in the NanoBiT assay, and the result was mostly negative (2 Gs-biased, 1 Gi-biased, 5 no effect; p.5). The 825 predicted complexes for Gq/11 and G12/13 are prospective in the weak sense that few reference structures exist (9 Gq/11 and 3 G12/13 experimental complexes, p.2) — but nothing about those predictions is validated.
state_metric: **NOT REPORTED.** No geometric criterion for receptor activation is defined, applied, or mentioned anywhere in the paper. There is no TM6 outward-displacement measurement, no TM3–TM6 (3.50–6.34) distance, no NPxxY/DRY microswitch check, no comparison of any predicted receptor against an inactive-state structure, and no active/inactive labelling of any model. The quantities that *are* measured are interface-placement and energetics metrics, and they are worth listing so the absence is not mistaken for sparse reporting: - **DockQ** (continuous, 0–1) of predicted vs experimental interface (p.7, Fig. 9A); - **fraction of native contacts** (continuous, 0–1) (p.7, Fig. 9B); - **pDockQ** ≥ 0.23 as a model-quality gate (p.13); - **pLDDT** ≥ 70 as a per-residue trimming gate (p.13); - **ΔSASA** ≥ 1500 Å² as a topology gate (p.13); - **Cβ–Cβ < 8 Å** (Cα for glycine) as the contact predicate — the paper's one true binary predicate, and it is an interface predicate: "We considered as contacts all the pairs of amino acids with less than 8 Å between their Cβ (Cɑ for glycine - see below), following standard practices employed for contact analysis in structural predictions46." (p.12); - **RMSD** of Gα core Cα after superposition on the GPCR 7TM core, and **RMSF** about the group centroid (p.15) — these measure *G-protein docking-mode* variability, not receptor conformation. In the schema's terms the paper is `binary predicate (8 Å contact) + continuous coordinate (DockQ / fnat / pDockQ / RMSD / ΔG)` **for the interface**, and `NOT REPORTED` for conformational state. Recording the latter as NOT REPORTED is the informative answer.
metric_saturation: **No numeric saturation in any arm reported.** DockQ and fraction-of-native-contacts are both bounded on [0,1]; the templates-on and templates-off violins in Fig. 9A/B sit around 0.65–0.70 and ~0.8 respectively with tails reaching neither 0 nor 1 (p.12), so neither floors nor ceilings. pDockQ is bounded [0,1] and its plotted range in Fig. 9C/D is ~0.0–0.6 (p.12). Rosetta REU and ΔSASA are unbounded. The **fingerprint vectors are binary by construction** (1 if contact present, 0 otherwise, p.13) — this is a design choice, not a saturating metric, but it means contact *strength* is discarded and any interface can only ever be described as present/absent. Figure-level truncation and pre-filtering are recorded in `hides`, not here.
directional_control: **Yes — one handle only: the identity of the co-folded G-protein α subunit.** The user chooses which Gα sequence to hand AlphaFold-Multimer alongside a fixed GNB1/GNG1 heterotrimer, and that choice is the only thing that differs between a "Gs complex" and a "Gi complex" model. p.13: "The human canonical protein sequences of GNB1 and GNG1 were used as the β and γ subunits, respectively." No other handle is available or used: **no ligand, no agonist, no nanobody, no state-annotated template, no state-filtered MSA, no seed control, no subsample depth.** Templates can be switched on or off (p.13) but are monomer-only and are not state-selected, so they do not steer state. Whether this handle actually controls the *receptor's* conformation is never tested — the paper only ever shows it changes the interface contacts (Fig. 9E, p.12). → tag `partner-driven`.
anti_memorization_design: **NONE.** There is no held-out set, no post-cutoff set, and no cutoff of any kind defined against AlphaFold's training data. The only date in the pipeline is the database download date — "The databases required to run AlphaFold-Multimer were downloaded on 12 January 2023." (p.13) — and the PDB harvest date, "over 360 complex structures deposited in the PDB (as of March 2023)" (p.2) with a SIFTS mapping from the "2023/01/28 update" (p.12). AlphaFold-Multimer v2.3's own training cutoff is never stated, so training-set membership of the 125 benchmark complexes is neither excluded nor quantified. → tag `no-anti-memorization`.
anti_memorization_control: **NONE RUN.** The templates-off arm (n = 125, `--max_template_date=01-01-1900`, p.13) is the nearest thing and it is a genuine, analysed control arm — but it ablates *template lookup*, not *weight memorization*, and the authors do not claim otherwise. With the training cutoff unstated, the 0.645 mean DockQ obtained without templates cannot be read as evidence against memorization; it is equally consistent with the complexes being in the training set. No arm addresses memorization.
confidence_as_discriminator: **Yes for interface plausibility, and partially validated; never used for conformational state.** Three confidence quantities gate the pipeline: AlphaFold's ranking score (0.2·pTM + 0.8·ipTM) picks 1 of 5 models (p.13); pLDDT < 70 residues are deleted before contact analysis (p.13); pDockQ ≥ 0.23 removes 118 of 975 models (p.13). The validation is a correlation against DockQ on the 125-complex benchmark, and it is reported as improving with filtering — Fig. 9C/D legends give default score r = 0.485 (full structure) → 0.618 (filtered), and pDockQ r = 0.480 → 0.621 (p.12), with the text claiming "Such a filtering scheme improves the correlation between prediction scores (pDockQ) and distance from experimental structures (DockQ) in the benchmark (Fig. 9C, D)." (p.7). That validates confidence as a proxy for *interface accuracy* only. It is never shown, or claimed, to discriminate conformational correctness. → tag `confidence-as-discriminator`.
stance: **`background` + `contrast` (provisional — the user's call).**
n_predictions: - *Samples per target*: **5** AF-Multimer models per complex, 1 retained by ranking score (p.13). Seeds, recycles and number of ensembles are **NOT REPORTED**. - *Targets*: 125 complexes in the benchmark (each predicted under 2 template conditions) + 996 GPCR–Gα pairs GPCRome-wide (p.7, p.13). - *Totals*: benchmark 125 × 2 × 5 = **1,250 models generated, 250 retained**; GPCRome 996 × 5 = **4,980 generated, 996 retained**, filtered to **825 analysed**. (The ×5 arithmetic follows from the stated protocol; the paper itself never states a total model count.) - *Rosetta arm*: 12 multistate designs per direction × 20 redocked poses = 240 redocked structures per design direction, 2 directions (p.14). - *Wet-lab arm*: 8 mutants + 3 WT titration conditions, n = 3–5 biological replicates each (p.8).
si_in_scope: **SI NOT HELD — and it matters.** The PDF contains no supplementary material. Absent from the corpus: **Supplementary Data 1** (all 362 PDB entries and the 125 representatives), **Supplementary Data 2–3** (GPCRdb and CGN residue mappings), **Supplementary Data 4** (CCKAR positions selected for design), **Supplementary Data 5** (the 825 predicted complexes), and **Supplementary Figs. 1–9**, which carry the UCM promiscuity comparison (S1), the unfiltered clustering control (S2), the RF/GF clusterings (S3), the per-mutant assay curves (S4), the RMSD clustering detail (S5), the class-A-only RMSD (S6), the relaxed-structure RMSD/RMSF (S7–S8) and the class-A-only binding energy (S9). Three of the paper's most important **controls** (S2, S6–S9) are therefore visible only as a p-value in the main text. Per-complex DockQ values are likewise unavailable — only the two means and two p-values in the main text are held. Source data files and the Zenodo/GitHub deposits are cited (p.15) but not part of this corpus.

venue: **bioRxiv preprint, not certified by peer review** — p1: "The copyright holder for this preprint (which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license." Tagged `preprint`.
title: **"Identifying and Addressing Systematic Data Leakage in Protein-Ligand Affinity Benchmarks"** (p1).
system: **general protein**, with three named sub-populations. The ChEMBL 36 meta-analysis is family-unrestricted and "cover[s] a wide variety of targets, including kinases, GPCRs, and metalloenzymes" (p4). The §3 case study is **GPCR** (five human muscarinic acetylcholine receptors M1–M5, p3). The FEP+ 4 benchmark is entirely **protein kinase** (TYK2, CDK2, JNK1, p38α, p4); the OpenFE leakage examples are kinase (BTK/LCK, p5) and tankyrase (TNKS2/TNKS1, p5, not a kinase). Table 2's sample (p5) spans kinases, GPCRs, HDACs, carbonic anhydrases, phosphodiesterases, collagenases, desaturases, prolyl hydroxylases and acetylcholinesterase.
n_targets: **dual, and must not be collapsed.** (i) FEP+ 4 = **4** targets (p4). (ii) OpenFE subset of Ross et al. 2023 = **39** targets (p4). (iii) §3 case study = **5** muscarinic receptors (p3). (iv) ChEMBL 36 meta-analysis = **6,115 assay pairs** across **2,689 papers**, from a pool of **59,552 assay pairs / 8,454 papers** (Table 1, p4); the number of distinct *targets* behind those pairs is **NOT REPORTED**. (v) Novelty-Tiered Affinity Benchmark: reported as assays and measurements per novelty bin (n_a 24 / 235 / 340 / 112 / 111; n_m 1108 / 6106 / 7383 / 2114 / 4396, Fig 4, p8), **total distinct targets NOT REPORTED**.
method_class: **benchmark-only** (critique of two existing benchmarks + construction of a new one), **plus** the training of a ligand-only ML baseline used as a leakage probe (§6 p6, Appendix C p11–12). No structure-prediction method is developed. The only co-folding *run* the authors perform is the two illustrative Boltz-2 poses in Fig 2 left (p6).
backbones: **Boltz-2** — used by the authors only to co-fold `lig_18633-1` with JNK1 and JNK2 for the Fig 2 left panel (p6). All other Boltz-2 and IsoDDE performance numbers in Fig 3 were **not rerun**: "Results for methods other than the baselines were taken from the IsoDDE report" (Fig 3 caption, p7). Boltz-2 [15], IsoDDE [16] and AQAffinity [17] are discussed as the targets of the critique (p2). No AF2/AF3/Chai/OF3/Protenix arm. **Not tagged `multi-backbone`**: at most two co-folding backbones appear, and they are not run head to head by these authors.
templates: **NOT REPORTED.** The Boltz-2 co-folding settings for Fig 2 are not stated anywhere in the paper or appendices. Everything else in the paper is sequence- and ligand-based.
msa_handling: **NOT REPORTED** for the Fig 2 Boltz-2 run. Note that MMseqs2 *is* used (p10, Appendix A) but for **sequence clustering to reproduce the train/test split**, not for MSA construction: `mmseqs easy-cluster fasta_seqs_for_clustering.fasta cluster_res cluster_tmp --min-seq-id 0.9 --cov-mode 0 -c 0.01`. Do not read that as MSA handling.
states_generated: **NOT APPLICABLE — no conformational states generated or scored.** The only structures produced anywhere are two Boltz-2 co-folded poses of one ligand shown for illustration (Fig 2 left, p6): "Predicted binding poses of lig_18633-1 co-folded with JNK1 (test set, orange, pIC50 = 6.75) and JNK2 (train set, gray, pIC50 = 6.56) using Boltz-2, with residues within 3.5 Å shown." The paper's output is a benchmark and a set of correlation statistics.
structural_priors_used: 1. **PDB reference entries used to map the OpenFE benchmark to targets** — p10: "Mapping the system group and system name columns to targets can be achieved via the `industry_benchmarks/input_structures/original_structures/*/subset_metadata.csv` files in the same repository and the `Reference PDB` entries." Deposited structures are used at *dataset-assembly* time, to identify which protein each measurement belongs to. 2. **Boltz-2 co-folding of the two JNK poses** in Fig 2 (p6) — a structure prediction used as visual evidence that two targets present the same binding environment. 3. **Binding-pocket similarity knowledge underpinning Table 3** (p6): "Targets with similar binding pockets to each FEP+ 4 test target, grouped by data split." The procedure by which "similar binding pockets" was determined is **NOT REPORTED** — see `unresolved`. 4. **Explicit refusal of a structural prior in the probe model**, which is the point of the probe — p11: "The baselines are ligand-only models trained to predict pIC50, pKi and pKd values from ligand features and a learned target representation, **with no structural information about the protein target**"; p6: "the protein target represented by a one-hot encoding that contains no protein structural information." 5. **Sequence, not structure, priors** for the split reproduction: ChEMBL 36 sequences plus UniProt for two missing test targets (p10). None of the above is a defect; it is recorded here rather than in `oracle_leakage` per the v3 rule.
oracle_leakage: **the corpus sense of the field — knowledge of deposited structures of a target state entering the pipeline — is essentially absent here, because there is no conformational pipeline.** Route by route: 1. **Structures used as input or template** — **NONE FOUND for the paper's own quantitative results.** The probe model takes no protein structure at all (p11, quoted above); the split is built from sequence clustering (p10). **NOT REPORTED for the Fig 2 Boltz-2 run** (p6), whose template/MSA configuration is never stated; that run produces no number, only a picture. 2. **State annotations from a curated database (GPCRdb / KLIFS / Kincore) driving templates or alignments** — **NONE FOUND.** The databases used are ChEMBL 36 [22], UniProt [30] and the OpenFE/protein-ligand-benchmark repositories (p10); none carries conformational-state annotation, and no alignment is state-filtered. Protocol described p10 (Appendix A) and p12–13 (Appendix D). 3. **Cluster labels derived from known states** — **NONE FOUND.** Clusters are MMseqs2 sequence clusters at `--min-seq-id 0.9` (p10); the novelty tiers are Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto bins over *ligands* (p8, p13). No cluster carries a state label. 4. **Hyperparameters, sweep ranges, seeds or stopping criteria tuned against the evaluation set** — **NONE FOUND for the proposed benchmark, PARTIAL for the FEP+ 4 / OpenFE arms.** For NTAB the validation set is a disjoint year band and the authors state why: "Since the validation set influences model development through early stopping and hyperparameter optimization, leakage across the test/val boundary would inflate reported performance in the same way as leakage across test/train" (p12), with "the best checkpoint selected by validation Pearson r" (p11). For the FEP+ 4 / OpenFE arms the baselines were "trained on ChEMBL 36 [22], which had been split following the FEP+ 4 and OpenFE benchmark methodology" (p6) and no separate validation protocol for those runs is stated — **NOT REPORTED**. One design choice touches the test set directly: "For targets absent from the training set, the embedding and bias of the nearest training target by protein sequence similarity were used" (p11), i.e. the test target's sequence identity selects which learned embedding is applied. That is the mechanism under study, deliberately, not a concealed leak. **No sweep range is reported at all** (Table 5, p12, fixes d = 2048, d_target = 256, n_hidden = 4 with no sweep description) — see `unresolved`. 5. **Success defined post hoc by RMSD or TM to a structure they had** — **NONE FOUND / NOT APPLICABLE.** Success is Pearson r (and MAE) against experimental affinity (Figs 3, 4, 7, 8). The single structural claim is qualitative and by eye: "The poses are virtually indistinguishable" (Fig 2 caption, p6) — no RMSD is computed or reported. 6. **Best/worst model labels assigned against a held reference** — **PRESENT, in the weak reporting sense.** The headline ligand-only numbers are "the best ligand-only model" selected *by its score on the benchmark being criticised*: p6, "On the FEP+ 4 test set, the best ligand-only model matched Boltz-2 and the physics-based OpenFE model at r = 0.66... On the OpenFE benchmark, the best ligand-only model achieved r = 0.36". Reading Fig 3 (p7), the best model differs between the two benchmarks — FP + mol desc (0.66) on FEP+ 4, Chemprop (0.36) on OpenFE, where FP + mol desc scores only 0.27. Same on the new benchmark: "the best ligand-only performance drops considerably from r = 0.61 to r = 0.14" (p8). All three baselines are always shown, so the selection is visible rather than hidden, but the abstract quotes only the maximum. 7. **Design-level oracle use — systems or inputs chosen because the expected answer is already known** — **PRESENT, and labelled design-level, not pipeline leakage.** Both demonstrative case studies were selected because the correlation was known in advance. p3: "This data was extracted from a single 1998 paper [21] in which the authors were optimizing a chemical series of antagonists specifically to be selective for the M4 receptor over the M1 receptor" — a series chosen for a family known to mirror. p5: "The JNK1/JNK2 case is the clearest example of leakage: the entire compound series appears on both sides of the split." p5 likewise selects "two specific subsets, 'merck' and 'miscellaneous'" out of a collection they say they investigated in full. This is standard demonstrative practice for an existence proof, and the authors back it with the unselected 6,115-pair census (Table 1, p4) and the full-sweep Fig 5 (p8); but the anecdotes themselves are chosen on the outcome. - **Separately: the paper's OWN definition of leakage**, which is what it measures, is affinity-value leakage across a protein-sequence-identity split — recorded in full under `central_conclusion` and `necessity_claims` below. Do not conflate the two vocabularies when querying this note.
prospective: **no.** Every number is retrospective: a re-analysis of two published benchmarks, a census of an existing database (ChEMBL 36), and a temporally split benchmark whose "prospective" character is simulated by a publication-year cutoff (train < 2022, val 2022, test ≥ 2023, p12). No compound was made or measured. The authors frame prospectivity as the *goal* the field is failing, not as something they achieved (p9).
state_metric: **NOT APPLICABLE** — no conformational state is called. The paper's metrics are continuous: Pearson r and MAE (Figs 3, 4, 7, 8). Two thresholds used as binary predicates are stated and justified: **R² ≥ 0.6** for "correlated" assay pairs (p4, criterion 4; justified as the same thing as r ≥ 0.77, p3) and **< 90% sequence similarity** for "dissimilar" targets (p4, criterion 3; justified as the value the criticised benchmarks use, p4).
metric_saturation: **YES, numerically, in one arm.** Per-assay Pearson r is bounded on [−1, 1] and in Fig 7 (p11) individual grey assay points sit exactly at **r = 1.00** (several) and at **r = −1.00** (one), i.e. the per-assay metric floors and ceilings on small assays. The authors recognise this and filter against it in the proposed benchmark: assays are retained only with "at least 10 unique compounds, a −log10 standard deviation of at least 0.5 across those compounds" because "Correlation coefficients against assays with insufficient compounds or low-affinity variations would be dominated by measurement noise" (p13). The *aggregate* means never approach the ceiling (maximum reported value 0.85, Fig 3 p7), so the headline numbers are not saturated. No axis break or truncation anywhere — see `hides` (Fig 3) for the figure-level defects, which are pooling, not saturation.
directional_control: **NOT APPLICABLE** — nothing is instructed to produce a state. The nearest analogue is the *handle on leakage*, which is the Tanimoto-similarity tier: the experimenter can dial ligand novelty from ≥ 1.00 down to < 0.35 and watch the ligand-only score fall (Fig 4, p8). That is a control on the benchmark, not on a model's output state.
anti_memorization_design: **YES — this is the paper's contribution.** The **Novelty-Tiered Affinity Benchmark**, built on ChEMBL 36, with two stacked barriers (p7–8, detailed p12–13): 1. **Temporal split by ChEMBL source-document publication year**: "assays from ≥ 2023 in test, 2022 in val, and < 2022 in train" (p7). The val band is separate precisely so early stopping cannot leak (p12). 2. **Ligand-novelty tiers by maximum Tanimoto similarity** (2048-bit Morgan fingerprints, radius 2) between each test compound and **all compounds whose earliest ChEMBL publication predates the cutoff** (p13). Exact-match compounds are broken out into their own bin (= 1.00). Bins and n (Fig 4, p8): **[0.00, 0.35)** n_a = 24, n_m = 1108; **[0.35, 0.50)** n_a = 235, n_m = 6106; **[0.50, 0.70)** n_a = 340, n_m = 7383; **[0.70, 1.00)** n_a = 112, n_m = 2114; **= 1.00** n_a = 111, n_m = 4396. 3. **Assay predictability filter** (p13): test/val assays kept only with ≥ 10 unique compounds, −log10 standard deviation ≥ 0.5, equality-relation measurements only, and **at most one assay per document**, keeping the largest — "to avoid biasing the benchmark with multiple near-identical series from the same experimental campaign". 4. **Source filters** (p12): ChEMBL max confidence score 9, binding assay type, single protein target, direct or homologous target mapping, Ki/Kd/IC50 only, mutant-sequence assays and flagged measurements excluded, all values on the −log10 scale. The cutoff is defined by **publication year of the ChEMBL source document**, not by a structure deposition date; the authors note this lets a two-step co-folding + affinity pipeline align both models' cutoffs (p12).
anti_memorization_control: **RUN, and analysed — but on the baseline only, never on the models under criticism.** The ligand-only baselines are run across all five novelty tiers (Fig 4, p8), against a temporal-split-only benchmark ("our best ligand-only method achieved r = 0.32, indicating that a temporal split alone is insufficient to prevent data leakage", p9), and against the assay-average binning variant (Fig 8, p13). **Not `UNPOWERED` in the main tiers** (n_a 24–340, n_m 1108–7383; the authors contrast this with 10–21 per bin in the Boltz-2 analysis, p11). Two qualifications: (a) the **[0.00, 0.33) bin of Fig 8 has n_a = 5** and a confidence band spanning roughly 0.0–0.4 — that arm alone is unpowered; (b) **Boltz-2 and IsoDDE were never evaluated on the leakage-controlled benchmark** — the paper reports no co-folding number on NTAB at all, which is the single largest gap in it (see `unresolved`).
confidence_as_discriminator: **NONE — no pLDDT, pTM or ipTM appears anywhere in the paper.** Model selection uses validation Pearson r (p11), and the two Boltz-2 poses in Fig 2 carry no confidence annotation (p6). Boltz-2's own affinity-confidence head is not discussed.
stance: **`threat` on standards + `precedent` on methodology** — provisional, the user's call. *Threat*: the paper's operative standard is that a generalisation claim is worth nothing unless a leakage-free floor is reported alongside it, and it demonstrates that both temporal splits alone (r = 0.32, p9) and sequence-identity splits at any threshold (Fig 5, p8) fail to establish one. Any generalisation claim we make on a sequence-identity-split or date-split benchmark is exposed to exactly this argument. *Precedent*: the novelty-tier construction (p7–8, p12–13) and the ligand-only-baseline-as-floor device (p6, p11) are directly adoptable, and the paper open-sources both data and code (p9). It is **not** `contrast`: the paper is not about conformational states and does not compete with our subject matter.
n_predictions: no sampling in the generative sense; the analogous quantities are: - **Targets**: FEP+ 4 → 4; OpenFE → 39 (p4). Muscarinic case study → 5 (p3). - **Measurements**: OpenFE → **873** in the version the authors used (the IsoDDE-cited release), vs **867** in the Boltz-2 release (p10, p11). FEP+ 4 measurement count **NOT REPORTED** (extracted from `00_data/ligands.yml` per target, p10). - **NTAB per-bin measurements**: 1108 / 6106 / 7383 / 2114 / 4396 across the five tiers, over 24 / 235 / 340 / 112 / 111 assays (Fig 4, p8). Assay-average variant: 747 / 16,753 / 11,437 over 5 / 546 / 374 assays (Fig 8, p13). Fig 7 reproduction buckets: 304 / 330 / 128 / 111 measurements over 16 / 21 / 11 / 10 assays (p11). - **Census**: 59,552 candidate assay pairs → 6,115 correlated pairs (Table 1, p4). - **Models trained**: three ligand-only baselines (Chemprop, FP + mol desc, mol desc only), each 100 epochs, best checkpoint by validation Pearson r (p11). Number of seeds or replicate training runs **NOT REPORTED**; uncertainty is bootstrapped over assays, not over training runs.
si_in_scope: **PARTIAL — SI NOT HELD for the census table.** The 6,115-pair table is represented in the PDF only by a 20-row sample (Table 2, p5): "The full table, as well as the scripts used to perform the analysis, are available in the supporting materials for this paper" (p4). Those supporting materials are not in the corpus. Everything else that carries a number — Tables 1, 3, 4, 5 and Figures 1–8 — **is in the PDF**, including all four appendices; the paper has no separate SI document beyond the census table, the Zenodo dataset (`10.5281/zenodo.19665374`) and the two GitHub repositories (p9). Per-target breakdowns of the Fig 3 bars (per-target r for the 4 FEP+ 4 and 39 OpenFE targets) are **not printed anywhere** — only size-weighted means.

year: 2026 (version posted 10 March 2026; p1)
venue: bioRxiv preprint — **not peer reviewed** ("which was not certified by peer review", p1). Tagged `preprint`.
title: Computed atlas of the human GPCR-G protein signaling complexes
system: GPCR (whole human GPCRome, non-olfactory + olfactory), each in complex with heterotrimeric G protein (Gα + GNB1 + GNG1)
n_targets: **801 receptors** (393 non-olfactory + 408 olfactory; "Fraction of unique GPCR (total=801)", p34; 393/408/13 in the Fig 1A workflow box, p28) × **13 Gα subunits** = **10,413 receptor–Gα pairs** (5,109 non-OR, p4; 5,304 OR, p22). 796 of the 801 entered the structural phylogeny (5 receptors >2700 aa excluded, p23). Generality claim is genuine at GPCRome scale but confined to one receptor family.
